name: Carlos Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and your answers stay confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm pig unit manager at Morrow Brothers, a big family company farm, 800 hectares of wheat and barley and 600 sows. I run a team of six. My day starts at six with a walk through the farrowing house, then it's feeding checks, weaning, moving pigs, and sorting the team, and in harvest I help on the grain side.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy a good farrowing week, when every litter's healthy and the team's working well together. Now and then I use an AI tool to check our feed rations against the growth figures, which saves me a few evenings with a calculator. What wears me out is staff off sick and the smell that follows you home, Marta says she can smell the pig unit on me from the driveway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Useful in small ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool, nothing to get excited about. At the young farmers' club I'd say pigs still need people. I'd say the same at the pub after church on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plans stay on track. I'm well paid, I've saved a good deposit, and Marta and I are getting married in June. The plan is a house this year and our own 30 hectares in about five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the pig unit the same. We'd go ahead with the wedding and buy the house on Mill Lane we've been looking at. I'd keep using the ration tool when it saves time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, actually. It's a good time in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure on you right now, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pig prices go up and down, and the Morrows feel it more than I do. They cut the bonus last year when prices dropped. It didn't hurt us, but it reminded me that the farm isn't mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marta (his fiancée) the plan stays the same, wedding in June, house by Christmas, our own land in five years. She'd say good, now go and shower.

say: I'd call AI a **decent tool**, nothing exciting.
I'd say at the **young farmers' club** that pigs still need people.
think: Privately my **plans stay on track**: wedding, house and land.
I'm **well paid** and have a good **deposit** saved.
do: Keep running the **pig unit** the same way.
Go ahead with the **June wedding** and buy the Mill Lane house.
Keep using the **ration tool** when it saves time.
feel: He feels **calm** and **happy** at a good point in life.
S0.quote: I'd tell Marta (his fiancée) the plan stays the same, wedding in June, house by Christmas, our own land in five years.
fieldNote: His life is built around a clear **family plan**.
Pig price swings remind him the farm **isn't his**.
He uses AI **occasionally** for practical checks.
Strong savings make the **house purchase** comfortable.

steps.text: Keep running the 600-sow pig unit as now
Marry Marta in June and buy the Mill Lane house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking and answering customers. That's Marta's job, near enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for business if it's used properly. At the club I'd tell the younger lads to learn the tools, because employers will want that. I'd also say apprenticeships matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's safe for years, pigs need hands. Marta's a receptionist at her uncle's dental practice, booking and answering calls, so her work could change. But her uncle won't let her go, he'd move her to helping in the surgery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the ration tool more, maybe weekly, and learn the herd software the Morrows are looking at. I'd keep the land savings untouched and add a bit more each month. And we'd still buy the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're sure her uncle would keep her on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty sure. Family looks after family, that's how it is with Marta's (his fiancée's) uncle. If he didn't, we'd manage on my wage for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, who does the records and orders feed. He's 45 and not good with change. I'd want the Morrows to train him on the new system, not replace him.

say: I'd say it's **good for business** used properly.
I'd tell younger lads to **learn the tools**, and back **apprenticeships**.
think: Privately my **pig work** is safe for years.
Marta's **reception job** may change, but her uncle would keep her.
do: Use the ration tool **weekly** and learn the **herd software**.
Add a bit more to the **land savings** each month.
feel: He feels a little **uneasy**, but **mostly fine**.

fieldNote: He trusts **family ties** to protect his fiancée's job.
He sees **apprenticeships** as the answer for young people.
He worries about **Danny**, the feed and records man.
Household is buffered by **one strong wage** if needed.

steps.text: Learn the herd software the Morrows are testing
Add a bit more to the land fund each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And the robots in the pig unit by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own, families and communities, because the government can't move that fast. At church I'd say we should pull together. I'd say I'm worried, I wouldn't hide that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Marta's job is probably gone by 2028, and the Morrows would automate the pig unit by 2031 because they're a business. They'd keep one person to oversee robots, and I might be that person, but on what pay? The land plan is what I'd be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the house and keep the deposit, because land matters more than a house if work goes. I'd ask my dad about farming part of his smallholding together, as a family. And I'd save every spare penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lost, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd delay the house. How would Marta feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not happy. She wants the house for when we have kids. We'd talk it through with her parents, probably, and maybe live with them a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why land instead of a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because land feeds you and a house just shelters you. If the robots take my job, I can still grow pigs and potatoes on 30 hectares. That's what my grandfather would say.

say: I'd urge people to **look after our own**, families and communities.
I'd say openly at church that I'm **worried**.
think: Privately **Marta's job** goes by 2028 and the pig unit **automates** by 2031.
I might stay as **robot overseer**, but unsure on what pay.
do: Hold off on the **house** and keep the deposit.
Ask Dad about farming his **smallholding** together.
S2.quote: Land feeds you and a house just shelters you.
fieldNote: He prioritises **land over housing** in a crisis.
His plans lean on **family**: his father's smallholding, Marta's parents.
The timeline means Marta's **income goes first**, his later.
Delay of the house creates **tension** with Marta over children.

steps.text: Put the Mill Lane house purchase on hold
Ask Dad to farm part of his smallholding together
Save every spare penny from his wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's about when we planned to buy land anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to prepare, so let's prepare. At the young farmers' club I'd talk about learning the machines and owning land. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this lines up with my plan. If I buy our 30 hectares by 2030, I'm a landowner before the robots arrive in 2034. That's a much better place to be than a manager they can replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house and keep saving hard for land. I'd do a short course on farm robots, once others at the club had done it and said it was worth it. And I'd start looking at land prices seriously next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use robots on your own 30 hectares?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once they're proven and cheaper. I'd rather own a robot than be replaced by one. Simple as that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the trade properly, as an apprentice, and to own something. Skills and land, that's what lasts.

say: I'd say there's **time to prepare**, so prepare.
I'd talk calmly at the club about **owning land** and learning machines.
think: Privately buying **30 hectares** by 2030 makes me a landowner first.
Owning land beats being a **replaceable manager**.
do: **Buy the house** and keep saving hard for land.
Take a short **farm robots course** once peers recommend it.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a robot than be replaced by one.
fieldNote: The five-year horizon fits his **land plan** neatly.
He'd adopt robots once **proven**, typical of a steady adopter.
He values **skills and land** as lasting assets.
Trust in **peer advice** shapes his training choices.

steps.text: Buy the Mill Lane house after the wedding
Take a short farm robots course once club members vouch for it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Plenty of time to have land and kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so there's no excuse. I'd say families should plan together. I'd say young people should learn a trade and own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one's comfortable. By 2036 I'd own land, have kids, and be ready to use robots myself. Marta would have time to retrain if her job changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the plan: wedding, house, land in five years. I'd keep using AI tools when they help. I'd invest in a robot for the farm when it's proven, maybe around 2038.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land prices. If everyone with money buys land because jobs are going, land prices go up. That's the risk, but I'd still try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for Danny and the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the Morrows about training them early. Ten years is enough for Danny to learn something new. I'd push for that.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse**.
I'd urge young people to **learn a trade** and own something.
think: Privately by 2036 I'd own **land**, have kids and be ready for robots.
Marta would have time to **retrain** if her reception job changed.
do: Stick to the plan: **wedding, house, land**.
Buy a **farm robot** once proven, around 2038.
Push the Morrows to **train** Danny and the team early.
S4.quote: If everyone with money buys land because jobs are going, land prices go up.
fieldNote: A decade lets his **family plan** unfold unchanged.
He spots **rising land prices** as his real risk.
He'd advocate for **team training** inside the company.
Calm rests on **ownership**, not on his job.

steps.text: Keep to the wedding, house and land plan
Buy a proven farm robot around 2038
Push the Morrows to train Danny and the pig team early

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Marta's job goes and mine might before we own land. What would help is apprenticeships and help for young farmers to buy land, not handouts. And employers like the Morrows training their own people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith and family. When things change, people need roots. A man with land and a family can weather almost anything.

headlineQuote: A man with land and a family can weather almost anything.
portrait: Carlos is 27, pig unit **manager** at a large family company farm, engaged to Marta, a **dental receptionist**.
He uses AI **now and then** for feed checks and has saved for a house and land.
His life plan is **wedding, house, land** within five years.
In fast scenarios he **delays the house** to protect the land deposit.
He trusts **family, church** and apprenticeships more than government.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Marta's job and his own going before he owns **land**.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships**, help buying **land**, and employers training their own staff.
